# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.

- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.

Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. 57	
58	// The endpoint a task's hand-off calls, resolved against the repo's config.
59	// Returns `{ name, url, tokenEnv, headers }` or `{ name, error }` — a task naming
60	// an endpoint the repo has not configured is a repo-configuration fact, reported
61	// where the operator reads it, never a crash.
62	export function resolveEndpoint(config, task) {
63	  const name = task?.decl?.invocation_endpoint ?? DEFAULT_ENDPOINT;
64	  const endpoints = config?.taskScheduler?.endpoints ?? {};
65	  const entry = endpoints[name];
66	  if (!entry) {
67	    return { name, error: `this repo's config declares no invocation endpoint "${name}" (taskScheduler.endpoints)` };
68	  }
69	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
70	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
71	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
72	}
73	
74	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
75	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
76	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
77	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
78	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
79	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
80	// more than a label event was.
81	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
82	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
83	
84	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
85	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
86	//
87	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
88	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
89	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
90	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
91	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
92	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
93	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
94	//                                         guess which.
95	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
96	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
97	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
98	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
99	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
100	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
101	    if (!token) {
102	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
103	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
104	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
105	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
106	    }
107	
108	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
109	
110	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
111	    try {
112	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
113	        method: 'POST',
114	        headers: {
115	          ...endpoint.headers,
116	          'content-type': 'application/json',
117	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
118	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
119	        },
120	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
121	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
122	      });
123	      let json = null;
124	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
125	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
126	        return {
127	          ok: true,
128	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
129	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
130	        };
131	      }
132	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
133	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
134	      return {
135	        ok: false, answered: true,
136	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
137	      };
138	    } catch (e) {
139	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
140	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
141	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
142	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
143	    }
144	  };
145	}

1	# wiki-growth worker
2	
3	One compile-once/refine-in-place research pass over the repo's product wikis (the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern):
4	read what the wiki already knows, research only what its own backlog flags, write it back cited. **Most runs
5	find little or nothing — no new citable material means no branch, no PR, and that is the documented good
6	outcome.** A padded or fabricated update is worse than none.
7	
8	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue; GitHub access is the session's
9	**GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`) — never `gh`/`curl`/a clone. "Default branch" below means the repo's
10	actual default branch. The wiki set is derived **structurally**: every `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under
11	`product-wiki/`, excluding the `product-wiki/product-requirements/` and `product-wiki/sample-data/` subtrees.
12	
13	There is no preflight: whether this run happens was decided by the task's **precondition** (it declines while
14	a PR carrying the **`product-wiki-growth` label** — the marker every PR of this family applies to itself —
15	sits open for review), so by the time you read this the round is granted. Your job is the research; label the
16	PR you open `product-wiki-growth` so the next round's precondition can see it.
17	
18	## Method
19	
20	1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
21	   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
22	2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
23	   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
24	   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
25	3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
26	   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
27	   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
28	4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
29	   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
30	   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
31	   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
32	   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
33	5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
34	   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, 140 characters each — about one line) — so a new insight
35	   that belongs at the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Each bullet is one
36	   finding in plain words: no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, and preferably something a reader
37	   who knows the field would *not* already assume. Judging obviousness is hard, so when in doubt keep the
38	   line rather than agonising — short and slightly obvious beats long and careful. Rewrite a bullet the run
39	   superseded (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone
40	   when the run changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a
41	   table of contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
42	6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
43	7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
44	   surfaced.
45	
46	## Stop condition
47	
48	Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.
49	
50	## Delivery
51	
52	A unique branch per run, commits touching only `product-wiki/**` minus `product-requirements/`, one
53	**PR — never a push to the default branch directly** — carrying the **`product-wiki-growth` label**. The
54	label is load-bearing: it is how the next run's precondition sees this PR at all, so a PR opened without it
55	will be stacked on by the following slot — label it whether or not the PR then lands.
56	Then hand it to the one delivery procedure (`deliver-pr.md`) and do what it says. PR body: the question(s)
57	researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.
58	
59	## Tracking
60	
61	Standing issue found by exact title **"Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth"** in the repo — found by
62	title, never by number, never opened/closed as state (open it if missing). One dated comment when a pass
63	**grew** (`grew (PR #N): <one line>`) or was **blocked** (`blocked: <why>` — the human-visible convergence for
64	a failed unattended run). Clean no-ops stay silent — the pack's freshness advisory is the prolonged-silence
65	observer.
66	
67	`agent_model: opus` — reading a wiki, judging which of its open questions is worth this run, and telling a
68	citable finding from a plausible one is the heaviest judgment in the task set.
69	
70	## What this worker must never do
71	
72	Edit `product-wiki/product-requirements/`; edit anything outside `product-wiki/`; create new wiki folders

# wiki-growth worker

One compile-once/refine-in-place research pass over the repo's product wikis (the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern):
read what the wiki already knows, research only what its own backlog flags, write it back cited. **Most runs
find little or nothing — no new citable material means no branch, no PR, and that is the documented good
outcome.** A padded or fabricated update is worse than none.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue; GitHub access is the session's
**GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`) — never `gh`/`curl`/a clone. "Default branch" below means the repo's
actual default branch. The wiki set is derived **structurally**: every `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under
`product-wiki/`, excluding the `product-wiki/product-requirements/` and `product-wiki/sample-data/` subtrees.

There is no preflight: whether this run happens was decided by the task's **precondition** (it declines while
a PR carrying the **`product-wiki-growth` label** — the marker every PR of this family applies to itself —
sits open for review), so by the time you read this the round is granted. Your job is the research; label the
PR you open `product-wiki-growth` so the next round's precondition can see it.

## Method

1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, 140 characters each — about one line) — so a new insight
   that belongs at the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Each bullet is one
   finding in plain words: no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, and preferably something a reader
   who knows the field would *not* already assume. Judging obviousness is hard, so when in doubt keep the
   line rather than agonising — short and slightly obvious beats long and careful. Rewrite a bullet the run
   superseded (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone
   when the run changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a
   table of contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
   surfaced.

## Stop condition

Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.

## Delivery

A unique branch per run, commits touching only `product-wiki/**` minus `product-requirements/`, one
**PR — never a push to the default branch directly** — carrying the **`product-wiki-growth` label**. The
label is load-bearing: it is how the next run's precondition sees this PR at all, so a PR opened without it
will be stacked on by the following slot — label it whether or not the PR then lands.
Then hand it to the one delivery procedure (`deliver-pr.md`) and do what it says. PR body: the question(s)
researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.

## Tracking

Standing issue found by exact title **"Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth"** in the repo — found by
title, never by number, never opened/closed as state (open it if missing). One dated comment when a pass
**grew** (`grew (PR #N): <one line>`) or was **blocked** (`blocked: <why>` — the human-visible convergence for
a failed unattended run). Clean no-ops stay silent — the pack's freshness advisory is the prolonged-silence
observer.

`agent_model: opus` — reading a wiki, judging which of its open questions is worth this run, and telling a
citable finding from a plausible one is the heaviest judgment in the task set.

## What this worker must never do

Edit `product-wiki/product-requirements/`; edit anything outside `product-wiki/`; create new wiki folders
(automation refines existing pages — a human creates a wiki deliberately); write an uncited claim; delete a
claim without a superseded note; leave a `## Key insights` header asserting what the body it heads no longer
says; pad a growth log, a header, or a wiki page to look productive; merge or approve its own
PR; schedule anything (no cron, no `schedule:` workflow); touch the shared canon.

How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:

- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.

## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference

`.claudinite-checks.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:

- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the dispatch issue.

## 2. Arm auto-merge

Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
it once this repo's required checks pass.

## 3. When the arm is rejected

- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
  PR's **head sha**:
  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;

    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or

1	// product-wiki task: wiki-growth — one research-and-refine pass over the repo's
2	// product wikis (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6). Worker: task.md.
3	//
4	// WEEKLY, not daily and not commit-gated: research arrives on the world's clock,
5	// not the repo's, and a nightly high-model pass economically pressures
6	// fabrication (the Karpathy LLM-wiki cadence). The `commits` signal is declared
7	// only so the precondition can note recent product-relevant movement in context;
8	// the run itself is scheduled by frequency, not triggered by a commit.
9	//
10	// The open-growth-PR gate lives HERE, in the precondition (DESIGN §12: the
11	// precondition is the ONLY decision point — it used to be a task.md preflight,
12	// which was the agentic phase deciding to skip a run its precondition had
13	// already granted). It is not subsumed by the scheduler: planDispatch guards at
14	// most one open dispatch ISSUE per (pack, task) — it never looks at pull
15	// requests, and a completed run closes its issue while leaving the growth PR
16	// open for review. This gate is the only thing standing between an unreviewed
17	// PR and a second round of research stacked on top of it.
18	//
19	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
20	
21	// The label the worker puts on every growth PR — the family marker this
22	// precondition declines on. task.md names the same string; keep them in step.
23	const GROWTH_LABEL = 'product-wiki-growth';
24	
25	export default {
26	  id: 'wiki-growth',
27	  frequency: 'weekly',             // fires at the weekly anchor (DESIGN §2) — the world's clock, not the repo's
28	  precondition_signals: ['commits', 'prs'],
29	  agent_model: 'opus',                   // open-web research + curation is the heaviest judgment in the task set
30	  expected_outcome: 'merged-pr',
31	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
32	  agent_execution_timeout: 2700,            // open-web research is the least predictable of the tasks — very generous
33	
34	  // The weekly slot is the trigger — a wiki grows on research availability, not
35	  // repo activity — EXCEPT while a previous round's growth PR sits unreviewed:
36	  // then this run is declined here, in code, rather than granted and abandoned
37	  // by the agent. The worker's own stop condition (no citable material → no
38	  // branch, no PR) remains the legal empty OUTCOME of a run that did happen.
39	  precondition(signals) {
40	    const openGrowthPr = (signals.prs?.open ?? [])
41	      .find((p) => (p.labels ?? []).includes(GROWTH_LABEL));
42	    if (openGrowthPr) {
43	      return {
44	        run: false,
45	        reason: `growth PR #${openGrowthPr.number} is still open (label ${GROWTH_LABEL}) — research waits for its review, so a second unreviewed round is never stacked on it`,
46	      };
47	    }
48	    const touched = signals.commits?.touchedPaths ?? [];
49	    const wikiMoved = touched.some((p) => p.startsWith('product-wiki/'));
50	    const context = wikiMoved
51	      ? ['The product-wiki tree moved in the window — spot-check any pages whose cited claims the change may have superseded.']
52	      : [];
53	    return { run: true, reason: 'weekly product-wiki growth pass', context };
54	  },
55	};

1	# product-wiki
2	
3	Agent-maintained market, user, and competitor research for EdFringeNow, kept as
4	self-growing wikis under this directory (compile findings once, refine in place,
5	cite everything). This tree is **walled off from the app code** — nothing in the
6	repo may reference `product-wiki/` except the reviewed distillation under
7	`product-requirements/`, so no code silently depends on unreviewed research.
8	
9	## What lives here
10	
11	- **`product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the wikis into
12	  product requirements. The only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
13	  reference. Never auto-grown.
14	- **`sample-data/`** — small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (created
15	  when first needed; never test fixtures).
16	- **Everything else** — wiki space. A wiki is a folder with a `README.md`
17	  carrying `## Sources`, `## Open questions`, and `## Growth log`. The weekly
18	  growth pass researches each wiki's own open questions and writes back cited.
19	
20	## Wikis
21	
22	- **[competitor-landscape/](competitor-landscape/README.md)** — the existing
23	  Fringe discovery/planning tools, split by which of the product's two questions
24	  they answer, and where each gap is.
25	- **[market-and-audience/](market-and-audience/README.md)** — festival scale, the
26	  overwhelm problem, and the two audiences the product targets: the live
27	  in-festival crowd and the trip planners.
28	- **[audience-divergence/](audience-divergence/README.md)** — where those two
29	  crowds' requirements pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the narrow
30	  spine they share.
31	- **[festival-season/](festival-season/README.md)** — the other Edinburgh
32	  festivals in August and across the summer: their scale, diversity, locations,

# product-wiki

Agent-maintained market, user, and competitor research for EdFringeNow, kept as
self-growing wikis under this directory (compile findings once, refine in place,
cite everything). This tree is **walled off from the app code** — nothing in the
repo may reference `product-wiki/` except the reviewed distillation under
`product-requirements/`, so no code silently depends on unreviewed research.

## What lives here

- **`product-requirements/`** — the human-reviewed distillation of the wikis into
  product requirements. The only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  reference. Never auto-grown.
- **`sample-data/`** — small illustrative assets a wiki claim points to (created
  when first needed; never test fixtures).
- **Everything else** — wiki space. A wiki is a folder with a `README.md`
  carrying `## Sources`, `## Open questions`, and `## Growth log`. The weekly
  growth pass researches each wiki's own open questions and writes back cited.

## Wikis

- **[competitor-landscape/](competitor-landscape/README.md)** — the existing
  Fringe discovery/planning tools, split by which of the product's two questions
  they answer, and where each gap is.
- **[market-and-audience/](market-and-audience/README.md)** — festival scale, the
  overwhelm problem, and the two audiences the product targets: the live
  in-festival crowd and the trip planners.
- **[audience-divergence/](audience-divergence/README.md)** — where those two
  crowds' requirements pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the narrow
  spine they share.
- **[festival-season/](festival-season/README.md)** — the other Edinburgh
  festivals in August and across the summer: their scale, diversity, locations,
  the six different shapes an "event" takes across them, and whether the data is
  reachable.

1	# Audience divergence — the live crowd vs the trip planners
2	
3	EdFringeNow now points at two decisions with two front ends: *Fringe Discover*
4	(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
5	`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").
6	This page exists to hold the evidence that **the two do not reduce to one set of
7	requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
8	narrow spine they genuinely share.
9	
10	It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
11	implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
12	`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.
13	
14	## Key insights
15	
16	- The two surfaces do not reduce to one set of requirements. That is the finding.
17	- The planner packs the day; the evidence says a good day is half empty.
18	- One sold-out flag: a fact for the live surface, a decaying guess for the planner.
19	- Live asks the user for nothing. The planner needs a CSV from a third-party extension.
20	- "When should I come?" has no live version — and no competitor answers it.
21	- What they truly share is small: the catalogue, the travel model, the promise.
22	- The plan-to-live handover is the one shared feature worth building. It does not exist.
23	
24	## The two crowds in a line each
25	
26	- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
27	  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
28	  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
29	- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
30	  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
31	  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
32	  festival long before it starts.
33	
34	They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
35	thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
36	leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
37	handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.
38	
39	## Where they diverge
40	
41	| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
44	| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
45	| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
46	| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
47	| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
48	| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
49	| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
50	| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
51	| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
52	| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
53	| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |
54	
55	## Requirements that actively conflict
56	
57	These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
58	Naming them is the point of this page.
59	
60	1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
61	   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
62	   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
63	   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
64	   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
65	   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
66	   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
67	   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
68	2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
69	   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
70	   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
71	   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
72	   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
73	   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
74	   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
75	   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
76	3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
77	   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
78	   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
79	   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
80	   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
81	4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
82	   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
83	   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
84	   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
85	   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
86	   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
87	   serve neither.
88	5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
89	   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
90	   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
91	   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
92	   and no profiled competitor answers it.
93	6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
94	   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
95	   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
96	   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
97	   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
98	   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
99	7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
100	   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
101	   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
102	   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
103	   than a map).
104	
105	## What the two genuinely share
106	
107	Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:
108	
109	- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
110	  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
111	  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
112	- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat
113	  counts beyond a sold-out flag. Neither surface may imply data we don't have.
114	- **The same emotional promise** — the overwhelm lifting. 37% of audiences
115	  reported struggling to pick a show; both surfaces exist to answer that, at
116	  different distances from the decision.
117	- **A handover, in one direction.** The planner's deliberate gaps are the live
118	  surface's demand. Nothing today connects them (no shared favourites, no "your
119	  plan says you're free until 19:00"), and that connection is the one place where
120	  a *shared* requirement would be justified.
121	
122	## Sources
123	
124	- [How to use your audience data with a purpose: the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (Thrive)](https://wewillthrive.co.uk/resources/case-studies/how-to-use-your-audience-data-with-a-purpose-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/) — a third of the audience lives in Edinburgh; two thirds of ticket buyers bought one ticket; 37% struggled to pick a show.
125	- [Fringe 2026 — How the Audience Has Changed (The Edinburgh Reporter)](https://theedinburghreporter.co.uk/2026/05/fringe-2026-how-the-audience-has-changed/) — months-ahead engagement; the CEO's "rule of thirds".
126	- [Edinburgh Fringe 2026: First-Timer's Planning Guide (Discover Edinburgh Fringe)](https://discoveredinburghfringe.com/en/blog/edinburgh-fringe-2026-first-timers-planning-guide) — two-to-three shows a day; walk-ups easy in week one, scarce in weeks two and three.
127	- [Ten tips for Fringe first-timers in 2026 (Edinburgh Festival City)](https://www.edinburghfestivalcity.com/inspiration/128-five-tips-for-fringe-first-timers) — leave travel time between venues.
128	- [Late night transport and 'live dashboard' could solve Edinburgh's festival accommodation crisis (The Scotsman)](https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/late-night-transport-and-live-dashboard-could-solve-edinburghs-festival-accommodation-crisis-5239090) — over half unable to find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute.
129	- [The 2026 Edinburgh Festival Fringe programme is now live (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/mixitup-with-the-2026-edinburgh-festival-fringe-programme/) — 4 June 2026 launch; 7–31 August dates.
130	- [EdFringe Favourites to CSV (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/edfringe-favourites-to-cs/ebbiecdkhoclnlgfibfhhnpfhmmgdbcc) — the third-party export path the planner's intake depends on.
131	- [Plan My Fringe — Help](https://www.planmyfringe.co.uk/Help.aspx) — the competing planner's constraint set (budget, walking speed, per-day max, minimum gap, meal and sleep minimums).
132	- [EdFringeNow — Fringe Discover product & experience brief (`docs/product-spec.md`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/docs/product-spec.md) — the live surface's stated inputs, outputs and zero-input target.
133	- [EdFringeNow — Fringe Planner README (`plan/README.md`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/plan/README.md) — the planner's intake, engine, controls, exports and three-day `localStorage` retention.
134	- [EdFringeNow — planner scheduling engine (`plan/lib/engine.js`)](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/blob/main/plan/lib/engine.js) — the earliest-finish-first greedy that maximises placed shows.
135	
136	## Open questions
137	
138	- **Is the shared person real, or two populations?** No evidence found either way
139	  on how many planner users are also in Edinburgh mid-festival. If the overlap is
140	  large, the handover (plan → live) is the highest-value unbuilt feature; if it
141	  is small, the two products should probably diverge further, not converge.
142	- **What should the planner optimise for?** "Most shows placed" is contradicted
143	  by the satisfaction evidence, but "leave a third open" has no measured optimum
144	  either. What does a *good* Fringe day look like, quantitatively?
145	- **How does availability actually decay between planning and August?** Nothing
146	  cited yet on sell-out rates by week or by show popularity — which decides how
147	  honest the planner can be about a plan made in June.
148	- **Does the accommodation constraint dominate date choice?** If it does, date
149	  scoring needs a second input the product doesn't have.
150	- **Is there a third crowd?** Artists, reviewers and industry are all in the same
151	  data with different needs (own-show scheduling, review runs); nothing here has
152	  looked at them.
153	- **Does the divergence extend to the scraper?** The live surface wants frequent
154	  refresh of status for today; the planner wants a stable whole-festival
155	  snapshot. Whether one data pipeline serves both well is unexamined.
156	
157	## Growth log
158	
159	- **2026-07-28** — initial seed, created deliberately after the owner asked for
160	  research covering both the live in-festival crowd and the trip-planning crowd
161	  without assuming a single requirement set. Compiled the divergence axes, the
162	  seven concrete requirement conflicts, and the shared spine, from the audience
163	  evidence gathered on the market-and-audience page plus the repo's two surfaces.
164	  Sources cited.
165	- **2026-07-29** — added the page's `## Key insights` header: seven terse lines
166	  distilled from what the page already says (the non-reducibility finding, the
167	  sharpest conflicts, the small shared spine, the handover). Header only: no
168	  claim, citation or open question changed.

8	
9	The field is not one field. The live/in-the-moment side has essentially one
10	incumbent; the planning side is crowded, and got noticeably more crowded for
11	2026.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- Nobody does live reachability. "Nearby now" stops at close and starting soon.
16	- The official app plans better than we assumed — calendar sync, offline, 200k downloads.
17	- Scheduling is table stakes: Plan My Fringe years ago, FringePlan now — plus iCal, sharing and edfringe basket handoff.
18	- Favourites import is taken. edfringeplanner does it. Only date-choice and the other festivals are still unclaimed.
19	- Fringe Finder plans around what is still on sale. That is the axis we are behind on.
20	- Half Price Hut tickets are in person only — live supply no app can see.
21	- Nobody here has used any 2026 rival. All of it is compiled from their own marketing.
22	
23	## The incumbents
24	
25	### Official Edinburgh Fringe app
26	
27	The Fringe Society's own app browses and books the full programme and serves
28	**both** of our questions — one weakly, one properly.
29	
30	- Closest to Fringe Discover: **"Nearby now"**, which uses phone location to show
31	  shows near you that are starting soon, plus **"shake to search"** for a random
32	  suggestion. Every published description of the feature (the official page,
33	  press coverage, the app-store listing, the build agency's case study) still
34	  frames it as *proximity + starting soon*. None mentions travel mode, travel
35	  time, or the user's **next commitment** — the slack calculation. No description
36	  of the 2026 edition claims otherwise.
37	- On the planning side it is stronger than this page previously recorded: **My
38	  Planner** saves shows by date and **syncs them to the user's own calendar**,
39	  alongside e-ticket QR codes, an **offline mode** for saved performances and
40	  tickets, and notifications when the next show starts.
41	- Reach: the build agency's case study reports downloads **surpassing 200,000** —
42	  a distribution no independent tool in this field is likely to match.
43	
44	The 2026 edition was again due to download in July 2026.
45	
46	### Plan My Fringe
47	
48	A schedule **optimiser**, and the closest existing thing to `/plan`. Its current
49	feature list overlaps ours almost item for item: a wishlist with per-show
50	ratings, then a schedule packing in as many shows as it can while honouring
51	**maximum budget**, **maximum shows per day**, **minimum gap between shows**,
52	**average walking speed**, and **minimum lunch, evening meal and sleep times**.
53	Its **"Fringe Trail"** chains shows to minimise walking and waiting and can be
54	viewed as an animated route on Google Maps; the website and app share one
55	wishlist, schedule and preferences; a **Recommendations** section (and a
56	"Fringey" chat) suggests shows using AI.
57	
58	What it does *not* appear to do: start from the user's **edfringe.com favourites
59	export**, or answer **"which dates should I come?"** — it optimises within a visit
60	the user has already decided on. That, rather than clash-free scheduling, is
61	where `/plan`'s remaining distinctness sits.
62	
63	### edfringe.com programme, filters and favourites
64	
65	The canonical catalogue, with filters (date/time, genre, free) and a personal
66	favourites list — strong for planning ahead, weak for the spontaneous "near me,
67	right now, still reachable" question. Favourites are the input `/plan` consumes;
68	extracting them as CSV is served by a **third-party Chrome extension** ("EdFringe
69	Favourites to CSV", maintained per festival year), not by any documented native
70	export.
71	
72	### Half Price Hut
73	
74	Same-day and next-morning **half-price** tickets, browsable online but purchasable
75	**in person only** at the Fringe Box Office (opening 12 August in 2026). A
76	price/spontaneity channel rather than a discovery-by-reachability tool — and a
77	reminder that a slice of live supply never appears in any app's inventory.
78	
79	### Reviews & word of mouth
80	
81	Outlets such as **ThreeWeeks**, plus star ratings on posters and Royal Mile
82	flyering, drive a large share of in-festival choice; discovery is heavily social
83	and serendipitous. Around 4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to edfringe.com
84	in 2025.
85	
86	## The 2026 planner-side field
87	
88	Several independent tools aimed squarely at the trip-planning crowd surfaced for
89	2026. None was profiled in this wiki's first pass, and together they change the
90	read on where the gap is.
91	
92	- **[Plan Your Fringe](https://planyourfringe.com/)** — "checks every single show
93	  against your dates, taste and budget and builds your day-by-day itinerary";
94	  free, independent, about two minutes end to end, itinerary downloadable as a
95	  PDF. Direct overlap with `/plan`'s output, without the favourites import.
96	- **[Fringe Finder](https://fringe-finder.netlify.app/)** — browse every 2026
97	  show, **track ticket availability**, and plan days with an **AI assistant** that
98	  builds a day-by-day plan from what is *still on sale*; describes itself as an
99	  official festival pilot (unverified). Availability-aware planning is the piece
100	  most tools skip — and the one axis where we are behind rather than ahead.
101	- **[Fringe Planner / edfringemap.com](https://edfringemap.com/)** — every show on
102	  one interactive map, filterable by day, genre, area, price and start time, then
103	  book. The closest thing to Fringe Discover's *map* surface, though as a
104	  browse-and-filter map rather than a reachability calculation.
105	- **[Ed Fringe Guide](https://edfringeguide.com/index.html)** and **[Another
106	  Fringe Guide](https://www.anotherfringeguide.com/)** — unofficial show finders /
107	  browsers, comedy-leaning.
108	- **[Edinburgh Fringe Planner](https://edfringeplanner.co.uk/)** — examined
109	  2026-08-09, and it is the one that matters. Its own one-line pitch is that it
110	  **"takes your favourites from edfringe.com and helps you work out what to do
111	  when"** — i.e. exactly `/plan`'s intake, the thing this page previously
112	  recorded as unclaimed. See the correction under *Where the gaps are*.
113	- **[FringePlan](https://fringeplan.com/)** — surfaced 2026-08-09 and not
114	  previously in this wiki. Free ("free for everyone, forever… no subscriptions,
115	  no ticket markups, and no hidden fees"). It takes a show list by pasted link,
116	  by name search, or "a whole list at once", pulling titles, venues, dates and
117	  performance times automatically; shows are marked high/medium/low priority;
118	  the schedule respects **travel time, meals and priorities**, and the user sets
119	  arrival/departure once so days can start from their hotel. Outputs are the
120	  broadest of any tool profiled here — a read-only share link, a **live iCal
121	  feed**, and a **markdown export**. Two features nothing else on this page
122	  claims: a bookmark that **sends a whole day of shows to an edfringe.com basket
123	  in one go**, and plans that **flag a delisted show or a moved performance
124	  rather than going stale**.
125	- **[planmyfestivals.com](https://www.planmyfestivals.com/)** — surfaced
126	  2026-08-02, self-titled "Edinburgh Festival Planner 2026". The plural
127	  "Festival[s]" naming is the only reason it is noted here rather than folded
128	  into the list above: it is the one 2026 entrant whose own name suggests it
129	  might plan across more than the Fringe, which would bear directly on the open
130	  question below. Not fetched or examined — its actual scope is unconfirmed.
131	
132	## The cross-festival field (almost empty)
133	
134	Every tool above is a *Fringe* tool. The city runs eight overlapping festivals in
135	August, and only one profiled competitor spans them:
136	
137	- **[Data Thistle](https://edinburghfestival.datathistle.com/)** — combined
138	  listings across the Fringe, International, Book, Jazz, Tattoo, Art, Film, Free
139	  Fringe, Free Festival and Fringe by the Sea, plus a commercial events API. A
140	  listings directory rather than a planner: no reachability, no itinerary, no
141	  favourites. The closest thing found to a multi-festival competitor.
142	- The **[Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/projects)**
143	  publishes a gallery of 13 apps built on it — Plan My Fringe, FringeFlow,
144	  TicketBadger, Frindr, myFestival, Festival Clock, Fringe Vibes and others.
145	  The data covers all 11 festivals; almost every app on it is named and framed
146	  around the **Fringe alone**. Nobody in the gallery claims cross-festival
147	  planning.
148	
149	Two caveats on how strong that reads. The gallery blurbs are the only evidence —
150	nobody here has used these tools, and the gallery may simply be stale. And a
151	cross-festival tool would not necessarily be *listed* there, since the API is not
152	the only source. Treat "the cross-festival claim is unclaimed" as the current
153	best reading, not a settled finding.
154	
155	## Where the gaps are
156	
157	**Live reachability — still open.** No tool centres full reachability: location
158	_plus_ travel mode/time _plus_ next-commitment slack ("can I see this and still
159	make my 7pm?"). The official app's "Nearby now" remains the nearest neighbour and
160	stops at proximity + starting-soon; Plan My Fringe models walking time, but for a
161	pre-curated plan. That live calculation is still Fringe Discover's distinct
162	position — see the product brief (`docs/product-spec.md`).
163	
164	**Planning — crowded, and the moat is narrower than it looks.** Clash-free,
165	travel-aware, meal-break-aware scheduling with per-day limits is **table stakes**
166	on this side of the field: Plan My Fringe has shipped all of it for years, and
167	2026 added at least three more itinerary builders.
168	
169	**Correction (2026-08-09) — the favourites-intake claim is taken.** This page
170	previously asserted that *no* profiled competitor starts from the user's
171	existing favourites list, and rested half of `/plan`'s remaining distinctness on
172	it. That is no longer supportable:
173	[edfringeplanner.co.uk](https://edfringeplanner.co.uk/) advertises precisely
174	that as its whole premise ("takes your favourites from edfringe.com"), and
175	[FringePlan](https://fringeplan.com/) accepts a whole pasted list in one go and
176	pushes a finished day back into an edfringe.com basket. The claim is left here
177	rather than deleted so the change of position is visible. What *survives* of it
178	is narrower and worth stating precisely: nobody was found taking the specific
179	**CSV produced by the third-party favourites extension**, and no competitor
180	documents where its favourites come from — so whether these tools use a native
181	export, the same extension, or a logged-in scrape is unknown, and that is now the
182	open question rather than the differentiator.
183	
184	What no profiled competitor still does:
185	
186	1. answer **"when should I come?"** — scoring date windows across the whole
187	   festival, the decision a visitor makes *before* any scheduling question
188	   exists. Re-checked this pass across Plan Your Fringe, Fringe Finder,
189	   edfringeplanner, FringePlan and Plan My Fringe: every one of them takes the
190	   visit dates as an **input** and optimises inside them. Still unoccupied.
191	2. plan across the **other seven August festivals** (see the section above).
192	
193	Those two, not the scheduler and no longer the favourites intake, are what a
194	planner-side requirement set would rest on. They are also a different claim from
195	the live surface's, which is why the two surfaces should not be reasoned about as
196	one product — see [audience-divergence/](../audience-divergence/README.md).
197	
198	## Sources
199	
200	- [Fringe app — Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://www.edfringe.com/experience/plan-your-visit/fringe-app/)
201	- [Edfringe on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/edfringe/id6450713971)
202	- [How the Edinburgh Fringe app works — including nearby event finder (The Scotsman)](https://www.scotsman.com/arts-and-culture/edinburgh-festivals/edinburgh-festival-fringe-app-4214702)
203	- [Edinburgh Fringe Festival app case study (equ)](https://equ.com.au/work/edinburgh-fringe-festival/)
204	- [Plan My Fringe — Edinburgh Fringe Scheduler](https://www.planmyfringe.co.uk/)
205	- [Plan My Fringe — Help](https://www.planmyfringe.co.uk/Help.aspx)
206	- [Plan My Fringe on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/plan-my-fringe/id1264802429)
207	- [Plan Your Fringe](https://planyourfringe.com/)
208	- [Fringe Finder — Edinburgh Fringe 2026 planner](https://fringe-finder.netlify.app/)
209	- [Fringe Planner 2026 — interactive map (edfringemap.com)](https://edfringemap.com/)
210	- [Ed Fringe Guide — unofficial Edinburgh Fringe show finder 2026](https://edfringeguide.com/index.html)
211	- [Another Edinburgh Fringe Show Finder](https://www.anotherfringeguide.com/)
212	- [Edinburgh Fringe Planner](https://edfringeplanner.co.uk/) — "takes your favourites from edfringe.com and helps you work out what to do when."
213	- [Edinburgh Fringe Planner — sign up](https://edfringeplanner.co.uk/signup)
214	- [FringePlan — Edinburgh Fringe Planner](https://fringeplan.com/) — clash-free schedule with travel time, meals and priorities; read-only share link, live iCal feed, markdown export, one-go edfringe.com basket, and stale-plan flagging.
215	- [EdFringe Favourites to CSV (Chrome Web Store)](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/edfringe-favourites-to-cs/ebbiecdkhoclnlgfibfhhnpfhmmgdbcc)
216	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe (programme)](https://www.edfringe.com/)
217	- [Half Price Hut — Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://www.edfringe.com/tickets/half-price-hut)
218	- [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Box Office](https://www.edfringe.com/experience/plan-your-visit/fringe-box-office/)
219	- [We've published our review of the year 2025 (edfringe.com)](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/weve-published-our-review-of-the-year-2025/)
220	- [ThreeWeeks (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ThreeWeeks)
221	- [Edinburgh Festival 2026 — combined listings (Data Thistle)](https://edinburghfestival.datathistle.com/)
222	- [Projects built on the Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/projects)
223	- [FringePlan](https://fringeplan.com/)
224	- [planmyfestivals.com — Edinburgh Festival Planner 2026](https://www.planmyfestivals.com/)
225	
226	## Open questions
227	
228	- **Hands-on verification is missing for every 2026 entrant.** All of the above
229	  was compiled from published descriptions and search results; no tool was driven
230	  end to end. Fringe Finder's "official festival pilot" claim in particular is
231	  unverified and matters — an official pilot on the planning side would change
232	  the competitive read. (Worse than it was on 2026-08-09: that pass tried to
233	  fetch fringe-finder.netlify.app, edfringeplanner.co.uk, fringeplan.com and
234	  planyourfringe.com directly and **every one was blocked by the network egress
235	  proxy**, so even their own pages were read second-hand through a search
236	  engine's index of them. Everything recorded about these four is their own
237	  marketing copy at one remove. A human on an unrestricted network could close
238	  this in twenty minutes.)
239	- **Does the shipped 2026 official app add travel-time or next-commitment logic
240	  to "Nearby now"?** Published descriptions still say proximity + starting soon,
241	  but nobody here has used the 2026 build. (Narrowed 2026-07-28 from "unknown" to
242	  "no published evidence of it".)
243	- **Does any tool expose real-time started / sold-out status** the way Fringe
244	  Discover's live status does? Fringe Finder claims availability-aware planning
245	  ("what's actually still on sale"); how live that is, and where it comes from,
246	  is unconfirmed.
247	- ~~**Does Plan My Fringe (or any planner) accept a favourites import?**~~
248	  **Answered 2026-08-09: yes — not Plan My Fringe, but edfringeplanner.co.uk,
249	  whose entire premise is it.** `/plan`'s intake advantage is gone. See the
250	  correction under *Where the gaps are*.
251	- **Where do these tools get the favourites from?** The successor question, and
252	  the one that decides whether anything is left of the intake position. No
253	  competitor documents the mechanism — native edfringe.com export, the
254	  third-party CSV extension, or a logged-in scrape are all consistent with what
255	  they say. If there is a native export nobody here has found, the
256	  market-and-audience page's intake assumption is wrong too.
257	- **Does FringePlan's "flag a delisted show or moved performance" mean it holds
258	  live availability?** It is the only claim on this page that sounds like
259	  post-plan freshness checking rather than a one-shot itinerary. If it is real,
260	  Fringe Finder is not the only tool on the availability axis.
261	- **Does anything else score date windows** ("when should I come?")? Re-checked
262	  2026-08-09 across five planners and found nothing — every one takes dates as an
263	  input. Narrowed from "or is that genuinely unoccupied?" to: still unoccupied on
264	  the evidence, but the evidence is five tools' marketing copy, not a survey.
265	- **Is anything actually planning across festivals?** The Listings API gallery
266	  says no, but the gallery is self-reported and possibly stale, and a
267	  cross-festival tool need not appear on it. Data Thistle lists everything and
268	  plans nothing — is that the whole field, or just the visible part of it?
269	  Checked 2026-08-02: a search for a cross-festival Fringe/EIF/Tattoo planner
270	  turned up no confirmed one, but did turn up **planmyfestivals.com**, whose
271	  name is the first hint of one — see above, unconfirmed.
272	- **Does Data Thistle's events API compete with us or supply us?** It is a paid
273	  feed over the same listings the free official API already gives away; what it
274	  adds is unexamined.
275	- "FRiNGE.Travel" surfaced in an earlier sweep and was never examined.
276	- What do users actually do in the "free hour" moment today — official app,
277	  posters, ask a friend? Still no cited behavioural source (the same gap is
278	  recorded on the market-and-audience page).
279	
280	## Growth log
281	
282	- **2026-07-22** — initial seed: profiled the official app (Nearby now / shake to
283	  search), Plan My Fringe (schedule optimiser + Fringe Trail), edfringe.com, the
284	  Half Price Hut, and reviews; framed the reachability gap. Sources cited.
285	- **2026-07-28** — reframed the page around both product surfaces after taking
286	  `/plan` into account, and split "where the gap is" into a live gap and a
287	  planning gap. Added the 2026 planner-side entrants (Plan Your Fringe, Fringe
288	  Finder, edfringemap.com, Ed Fringe Guide, Another Fringe Guide, Edinburgh
289	  Fringe Planner); expanded Plan My Fringe's current feature list (budget,
290	  walking speed, per-day max, minimum gap, minimum lunch/dinner/sleep, AI
291	  recommendations) and recorded that it neither imports favourites nor chooses
292	  dates; recorded the official app's My Planner / calendar sync / offline mode
293	  and its 200k+ downloads; noted the third-party favourites-CSV extension and the
294	  Half Price Hut's 2026 opening date. Narrowed the "2026 app Nearby now" open
295	  question rather than closing it. Requirements implication (planner-side
296	  requirements resting on favourites-intake and date-choice, not on scheduling)
297	  left for human review.
298	- **2026-07-29** — added the page's `## Key insights` header: seven terse lines
299	  distilled from what the page already says (the live-reachability gap, the
300	  official app's planning strength, scheduling as table stakes, the two
301	  unclaimed claims, the availability axis, in-person supply, the verification
302	  gap). Header only: no claim, citation or open question changed.
303	- **2026-07-31** — added the cross-festival field, found while researching the
304	  other Edinburgh festivals: Data Thistle (combined listings across ten
305	  festivals plus a paid events API — a directory, not a planner) and the
306	  official Listings API's gallery of 13 apps, almost all Fringe-only despite the
307	  data covering all 11 festivals. Recorded the evidence's weakness (self-reported
308	  blurbs, possibly stale, not exhaustive) rather than claiming the field empty.
309	  Key insight 4 rewritten from two unclaimed claims to three — the other seven
310	  August festivals joins favourites-import and date-choice. Two open questions
311	  added. Requirements implication left for human review — see the
312	  festival-season page and the multi-festival design proposal.
313	- **2026-08-09** — worked the page's top open question (hands-on verification of
314	  the 2026 entrants) and it cost the page a claim. Examined the two planners left
315	  unexamined: **edfringeplanner.co.uk**, whose stated premise is taking the
316	  user's edfringe.com favourites, and **FringePlan** (fringeplan.com), new to
317	  this wiki — travel-time-, meal- and priority-aware scheduling plus a live iCal
318	  feed, markdown export, share links, a one-go edfringe.com basket handoff, and
319	  plans that flag delisted or moved performances. Together they supersede this
320	  page's "no profiled competitor starts from the user's existing favourites list"
321	  claim, which is corrected in place with the reason kept rather than deleted;
322	  what survives of it is narrowed to the unknown *mechanism* of their import.
323	  Re-checked the date-choice claim across five planners and it held — every one
324	  takes dates as an input — so that question is narrowed, not closed. Key
325	  insights 3 and 4 rewritten; insight 4 goes from three unclaimed claims to two.
326	  Recorded honestly that all four target sites were blocked by the network
327	  egress proxy this pass and were read second-hand via search-engine indexing of
328	  their own pages, which makes the verification gap worse, not better. Two open
329	  questions added (favourites mechanism; whether FringePlan's stale-plan flagging
330	  implies live availability). Requirements implication — a planner-side
331	  requirement set can no longer rest on favourites intake, leaving date-choice
332	  and cross-festival — left for human review.
333	- **2026-08-02** — spot-checked the "is anything planning across festivals"
334	  open question with a fresh web sweep: found two 2026 entrants not previously
335	  profiled, FringePlan (a Fringe-only day planner, close to Plan My Fringe /
336	  Plan Your Fringe) and planmyfestivals.com, whose plural naming is the first
337	  candidate found whose own branding suggests cross-festival scope — added both
338	  to the 2026 planner-side field with the caveat that neither was fetched or
339	  examined hands-on, so planmyfestivals.com's actual scope stays an open
340	  question rather than a finding. Header unchanged: neither addition changes the
341	  page's top-line read (planning side crowded and Fringe-only; cross-festival
342	  field still effectively empty until verified otherwise).
